question: What is the primary purpose of a urinary catheter?

options.A: To deliver fluids directly into the kidneys
options.B: To prevent the formation of kidney stones
options.C: To drain urine from the bladder
options.D: To measure the capacity of the ureters

explanation: A catheter is a flexible tube inserted through the urethra specifically to allow urine to drain out of the bladder when a patient cannot do so naturally. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why do nurses try to avoid using a urinary catheter unless it's truly necessary?

options.A: It brings a high risk of introducing bacteria into the urinary tract
options.B: It is extremely painful for every patient who receives one
options.C: It requires surgical removal by a urologist
options.D: It permanently weakens the bladder muscles within hours

explanation: You got it! Because catheters bypass the body's natural defenses, they easily let germs in, making infections a big risk. That's why we only use them when we really have to.

question: Which body feature makes female patients more likely to get a catheter-related urinary tract infection?

options.B: A larger bladder capacity than males
options.C: An absence of a muscular sphincter
options.D: A shorter urethra close to the anal opening

explanation: Spot on! The female urethra is quite short and sits very close to the anus, giving bacteria a short and easy path straight into the bladder.

question: How is putting a catheter into a male patient different from a female patient?

options.A: It lacks a sphincter muscle, making insertion completely effortless
options.B: It opens directly into the abdominal cavity
options.C: It is longer and has natural curves that require careful maneuvering
options.D: It is wider, requiring much larger catheter sizes

explanation: Exactly! The male urethra is longer and travels through the prostate, so you have to gently navigate a few natural bends during the procedure.

question: What keeps a Foley catheter securely in place inside the bladder?

options.A: A flexible wire attached to the belly wall
options.B: External adhesive tape on the thigh
options.C: Natural suction created by the drainage bag
options.D: A water-filled balloon at the tip

explanation: Correct! Once the catheter is inside the bladder, sterile water fills a tiny balloon at the end, acting like an anchor so it doesn't slip out.

question: When would you choose a simple straight catheter instead of a permanent Foley catheter?

options.A: When the patient is unconscious in the intensive care unit
options.B: When a patient needs periodic bladder emptying without a permanent bag
options.C: When the patient has a severe urethral blockage
options.D: When long-term continuous monitoring of hourly urine output is required

explanation: You nailed it! Straight catheters are popped in to drain the bladder and taken right back out, which lowers the risk of infection compared to leaving a tube in all day.

question: Which of these is a valid medical reason to put in an indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: General urinary incontinence with no skin breakdown
options.B: To make things easier for nursing staff during busy night shifts
options.C: Accurate hourly urine output measurement in a critically ill patient
options.D: The patient prefers not to get up to use the toilet at night

explanation: Spot on! We only use indwelling catheters when there is a strong medical need, like closely tracking kidney function in very sick patients.

question: A patient with an enlarged prostate hasn't peed in eight hours and has severe lower belly pain. What should you do first?

options.A: Encourage the patient to drink more water to flush the system
options.B: Administer a mild oral water pill (diuretic)
options.C: Prepare equipment for urinary catheterisation as ordered
options.D: Apply a warm compress to the lower back and wait two hours

explanation: Great thinking! When urine gets trapped because of an enlarged prostate, getting it out with a catheter right away relieves the painful pressure.

question: What common allergy must you always check for before using a standard urinary catheter?
explanation: You got it! Many standard catheters contain latex, which can cause severe allergic reactions. Always check your patient's history and grab a silicone one if they are allergic!

question: Why is it helpful to feel (palpate) the patient's lower belly before doing a catheterisation?

options.A: To stimulate the urethral sphincter to open
options.B: To check if the kidneys are infected
options.C: To measure the exact length of the urethra
options.D: To confirm the presence of a full, distended bladder

explanation: Spot on! Feeling the lower belly (suprapubic area) lets you check if urine is actually backed up and trapped in the bladder, confirming you really need to catheterize.

question: In what direction should you clean a female patient's perineal area before putting in a catheter?
explanation: Correct! Always wipe from front to back (toward the back passage) so you don't drag any germs from the anus toward the urethral opening.

question: In male patients, why must you push the catheter a bit further in even after urine first starts to flow?

options.A: To clear any leftover bacteria sitting in the outer urethra
options.B: To make the drainage bag fill up much faster
options.C: To stretch the urethral muscle and reduce future spasms
options.D: To ensure the retention balloon is completely inside the bladder before inflating it

explanation: Spot on! If you inflate the balloon while it's still stuck in the narrow urethra instead of the open bladder, it causes terrible pain and injury.

question: Where must the urine drainage bag be placed at all times?

options.B: Resting directly on the patient's chest
options.C: Hanging from the top of the bed frame
options.D: Below the level of the bladder

explanation: You got it! Gravity is our friend here. Keeping the bag lower than the bladder keeps urine flowing smoothly downward and stops dirty urine from washing back up.

question: What is the main danger of disconnecting the catheter tubing from the drainage bag?

options.A: It breaks the closed system and lets bacteria enter
options.B: It triggers severe allergic reactions to the plastic
options.C: It causes immediate permanent damage to the urethral sphincter
options.D: It creates high pressure that bursts the balloon

explanation: Spot on! Keeping the drainage system sealed and closed is the single best way to protect your patient from getting a catheter-associated infection.

question: What should you check first if a patient with a catheter suddenly stops passing urine?

options.A: Pull the catheter out right away and put in a new one
options.B: Give a fast dose of an intravenous water pill
options.C: Check the tubing for kinks, twists, or someone lying on it
options.D: Call the doctor to report total kidney failure

explanation: Great nursing instinct! Most of the time, urine stops flowing simply because the tube is bent or pinched. Always check the lines first!

question: Which sign is a strong indicator of a catheter-associated urinary tract infection?

options.C: Bright red blood in the stool
options.D: Sudden swelling of the lower legs

explanation: You nailed it! When urine turns cloudy, smells bad, or the patient feels feverish and uncomfortable, it usually points to a brewing infection.

question: How do you deflate the retention balloon before taking out a Foley catheter?

options.A: Puncture the outer catheter wall with a large needle
options.B: Cut the balloon valve tubing with surgical scissors
options.C: Inject more water to pop the balloon safely inside the bladder
options.D: Attach a syringe to the inflation port and draw out all the water

explanation: Spot on! Hooking up a syringe and pulling out the exact amount of water that was put in ensures the balloon collapses completely before you slide the tube out.

question: What is an important task to carry out after a patient's urinary catheter is removed?

options.A: Keep the patient on strict bed rest for a full day
options.B: Monitor and measure the time and amount of their first pee
options.C: Give routine antibiotic pills to every patient
options.D: Restrict fluid intake for twelve hours to give the bladder a rest

explanation: You got it! Watching to see that they successfully pee within a reasonable time proves their bladder is waking up and working normally after catheter removal.
